changes.before: Implement parseBody(text). Match the worked contract and the changed-input checks without modifying the supplied input values.
changes.after: Return a clear failure result when JSON text cannot be read.

before: JSON parsing turns text into a JavaScript value. Invalid syntax causes JSON.parse to throw. A request handler needs an explicit failure path.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.
try contains the operation that can fail. catch handles a parsing failure. Successful parsing can still produce null, a number, or an array; it does not prove a valid request shape.

Read the function call parseBody("{\"minutes\":5}") from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, parseBody runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
The text null parses successfully. Does that prove it is a valid note object? Parsing verifies syntax. A later validator must check the value required by the application.
after: JSON is a text format used to send or save data. JSON.parse reads that text and turns it into a JavaScript value. Incorrect JSON syntax makes it throw an error.
try marks work that may throw. catch handles a thrown error. This lets parseBody report failure instead of letting a parsing error escape from the function.
When parsing succeeds, return an object with ok: true and the parsed value. When parsing fails, return {ok: false}. The caller can check ok before using value.

Valid JSON can contain null, a number, or an array, as well as an object. Parsing only checks whether the text follows JSON's rules. Later code must still check that the value has the fields the app needs.
Complete parseBody(text) using try and catch. Keep every successfully parsed value, including null. Return the failure object for invalid JSON text without changing the input.
